TEXT: The top result is the Hacker News thread for the article "Cleaning up after AI rockstar developers" (codingwithjesse.com), posted about 132 days ago. I couldn't open the thread itself, so this summary is based only on the search snippets.
- Speed is the main concern. One commenter argues that AI-generated codebases can grow far faster than human teams could build them, so years of accumulated mess can appear in weeks. (the speed at which AI-generated codebases grow is far in excess of what human developers can achieve. What took years to accumulate in the past can be produced in a few days/weeks.)
- Blame goes to management and process. A common view is that the fix is to stop messy code from being merged, not to clean it up afterward. One reply says the answer is to make the author clean up their own mess, and that if you let it happen, it'll happen 100x as fast.
- Skepticism about the article. One commenter asked whether the article's "cleaning up after hundreds of AI rockstars" part reflects a real experience, saying they would expect much more swearing if it did.
- Commercial angle. A separate HN thread, "We charge $10k a week to delete AI-generated code," shows that refactoring AI-generated codebases is now a paid service. The poster's firm, Slopfix, says it commits to a reduction target up front, and the client pays in proportion to how much of it they hit.

TEXT: The quote traces to a launch by a three-person team called Slopfix, posted on Hacker News. Fixed-price, outcome-based service. Slopfix charges $10,000 for one week of work and gets paid according to how much code it deletes. Its founder says the client pays in proportion to how much of [the reduction target] the team hits. Uses AI coding agents, human-led. Analyzes clients' repos for free and walks away if it decides it can't make a dent. Example: cutting a 100,000-line project down to 35,000. Two-week warranty on previously working components. Clients keep a CLAUDE.md file, lint rules, CI checks. Tom's Hardware links to GitClear data on duplicated code blocks. WebProNews describes a similarly priced $10,000-per-week service called Pull; less specific, treat as separate or derivative.
